Package com.egradx.auth.security

Interface EgradxPermissionResolver

All Known Implementing Classes:
EgradxDefaultPermissionResolver
public interface EgradxPermissionResolver
Resolves a user's current identity/organization/authorities from the database, deliberately ignoring whatever an access token's own claims say — this is what makes a role reassignment or a permission edit take effect on a user's very next request instead of their next login. See EgradxDefaultPermissionResolver for the actual logic; organizationId passed in here comes from the token (identity/ session-scoping only, non-authoritative), but the role and authorities for that organization are always looked up fresh.

  • Method Details

    • resolve

      Optional<EgradxResolvedPermissions> resolve(UUID userId, UUID organizationId)
      Returns:
      empty if the user no longer exists, is deactivated, or (when organizationId is non-null) that organization has been suspended — any of which should be treated as "not authenticated", not merely "no authorities"

    • resolve

      default Optional<EgradxResolvedPermissions> resolve(UUID userId, UUID organizationId, Instant issuedAt)
      As resolve(UUID, UUID), for a token issued at issuedAt — which is refused (empty) if the person's sessions were cut off after it was issued (password changed or reset, "sign out everywhere"). The authentication filter calls this one.

      The default ignores issuedAt, so a resolver written before this existed keeps working — without honouring the cut-off for access tokens. Refresh tokens are cut off regardless. EgradxDefaultPermissionResolver honours it.

    • resolve

      default Optional<EgradxResolvedPermissions> resolve(UUID userId, UUID organizationId, Instant issuedAt, UUID sessionId)
      As resolve(UUID, UUID, Instant), for a token of session sessionId (its sid) — which is refused (empty) if that session has ended (signed out, ended from another device, a refresh token reused) or expired. The authentication filter calls this one.

      The default ignores sessionId, so a resolver written before sessions existed keeps working — without ending one session's access tokens before they expire. EgradxDefaultPermissionResolver honours it.
